table.brief: i18n string table: Key (like checkout.button.confirm) / English / 中文 / 日本語 / العربية — five columns of short UI strings

understanding.purpose: Compare checkout interface strings across four languages, using stable keys to identify each message.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the key column to find a message, then read across its row to compare translations. Each row should remain a clear unit even when translations wrap.
groups: English, 中文, 日本語, and العربية are parallel translations of the same message and should have a comparable visual role.
Key is the row identifier and needs enough width for the longest unbroken identifier.
may_wrap: Translation phrases at natural word or character boundaries
Shorter translations can remain on one line while longer translations use the row height created by another language.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Start from r2A and give Chinese 5px more to fit the empty-cart string and shorten the email message. Keep Japanese at 130px to preserve its two short single-line strings; take the extra width from English and Arabic, where the shown phrases already wrap.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Refine r0B by protecting the key and keeping English relatively wide, while returning some space to Chinese. This tests whether its compact English phrases can coexist with clearer identifiers.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Test a larger Chinese column alongside a generous Japanese column, using the height already created by long translations to accommodate English wrapping. This may improve the balance of the CJK text without repeating r0C's very narrow Chinese column.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Give Arabic substantially more room to test whether the shipping range stays together. Retain the full key width and distribute the reduction across the other translations.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keep the useful Chinese and Japanese fit thresholds while allowing “Search products” to stay on one line. Test whether the narrower Arabic column still wraps its longer phrases comfortably.

bad.name: r2B
bad.note: Start from r1A and move 15px from Japanese to Arabic. This preserves r1A's English and Chinese widths while testing a more balanced treatment of the Arabic shipping phrase.
bad.why: The Japanese confirmation and empty-cart strings each leave a single character on a second line, making two short rows unnecessarily ragged.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Give English enough additional room to test whether Search products stays on one line, while increasing Arabic from the current designs. Use a narrower Japanese column because its longest message already determines a three-line row.
bad.why: The Japanese confirmation and empty-cart strings each leave a single character on a second line; the narrow Chinese column also strands a character in the empty-cart row.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Give Japanese more room for its long email message while retaining the Chinese empty-cart fit. Test whether the gain in Japanese line breaks justifies a narrower English column.
bad.why: The narrow English column breaks the short confirmation into two lines and the shipping estimate into three, leaving a lone word on the last line.

rationale: r3A keeps the keys intact and gives the four translations a balanced share of the remaining width. Its Chinese empty-cart and error strings fit more cleanly than in r2A, while the Arabic error occupies two lines rather than three as in r1C. The Japanese column is wide enough to keep both short opening strings on one line.

general: Protect identifying columns from breaking when readers need to scan and match rows.
Give comparable columns widths based on their content and wrapping behavior, rather than forcing equal widths.
Judge line breaks within individual cells as well as overall row height; a single stranded character or word can make a row harder to scan.
specific: The long unbreakable keys need at least 227px including padding and border.
In these renders, 130px for Japanese keeps the two short opening strings on one line, while 125px leaves a single character on a second line.
The wider Arabic column in r3A keeps the error message to two lines.

tradeoffs: r3B keeps the English search string on one line, but its narrower Arabic column wraps the error message into three lines. r1C gives Japanese more room, but makes the same Arabic tradeoff.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around r3A, not independently rendered thresholds. They describe one-column adjustments with the other columns adjusted proportionally to stay within 719px; rounding and browser line-breaking can change the result. Designers may also weigh a single-line English search string more heavily than the shorter Arabic error.

critique.good: The translations have a fairly balanced visual presence, and the confirmation and cancellation rows are compact. Most wrapped phrases remain easy to follow across their rows.
critique.problems: The longest key breaks with a lone final letter on the next line, making the identifier harder to scan. The Chinese empty-cart message also leaves a single character on its second line, while the search row gains height partly because the English phrase wraps.
critique.cause: The 225px key column provides 204px of text space, less than the stated 206px needed. The 109px Chinese and 124px English columns are narrow enough to trigger those wraps.

critique.good: The wider English column keeps the empty-cart and search messages on one line, making those entries easier to scan. The table retains the same overall height as r0A.
critique.problems: The longest key still breaks before its final letter. Chinese has a single-character continuation in the empty-cart row, and the long error message is densely wrapped across three lines in Chinese, Japanese and Arabic.
critique.cause: The 225px key column is 2px short of the stated intact width. The 148px English allocation takes space from the 99px Chinese and 131px Japanese columns.

critique.good: The wider Japanese and Arabic columns give those translations more room; the Arabic error message takes two lines rather than three, and Japanese shipping fits on one line.
critique.problems: The longest key still splits. English confirmation wraps despite being short, and the shipping range splits across lines in English. The narrow Chinese column also creates several short lines. These wraps make the table taller and weaken the rhythm of rows as units.
critique.cause: The 225px key column is too narrow for the longest identifier. The 111px English and 94px Chinese columns give up too much space to the 158px Japanese and 129px Arabic columns.

critique.good: The key column keeps every identifier intact, and the translation columns have a reasonably balanced rhythm. Chinese cart text stays on one line, and the headers are clear.
critique.problems: The Arabic shipping range is split between lines, making the numbers harder to read together. English search wraps into two short lines, while the Japanese shipping text leaves a single character on its second line.
critique.cause: The 111px Arabic column is too narrow for the range in its surrounding phrase. English has 125px, while Japanese has 140px.

critique.good: The 142px English column keeps Search products on one line, and all keys and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: Chinese cart text ends with a single character on a second line, and the Chinese error takes three lines. The Arabic shipping range is split across lines, and Japanese shipping ends with a lone character.
critique.cause: The extra English width comes partly from reducing Chinese to 105px and Japanese to 134px. Arabic remains narrow at 110px.

critique.good: The 120px Chinese column keeps the cart message on one line and the error to two lines. The key column is intact, and Japanese has slightly more room than in the other designs.
critique.problems: The Arabic shipping range is split across lines. English search wraps, and Japanese shipping still leaves one character on its second line. The extra Japanese width does not reduce the tallest row.
critique.cause: Arabic receives only 109px and English 119px; Japanese receives 143px but remains just short of fitting its shipping message on one line.

critique.good: The key column keeps every identifier intact, and all headers are clear. The Japanese confirmation and empty-cart strings fit on one line, giving the table a compact, readable rhythm. Arabic has enough room for natural phrase wrapping.
critique.problems: The Chinese empty-cart string leaves a single character on its second line, and the Chinese email message takes three lines. English search wraps despite being a short phrase.
critique.cause: The 110px Chinese column is just too narrow for the complete empty-cart string; the 121px English column is too narrow for “Search products.”

critique.good: The 115px Chinese column keeps the empty-cart string on one line and reduces the email message to two lines. Keys remain intact, and the translation columns have a reasonably even visual weight.
critique.problems: Both Japanese confirmation and empty-cart strings strand a single character on a second line, making the first two rows taller and less balanced. English search also wraps.
critique.cause: At 125px, Japanese is slightly narrower than the 130px in r2A, crossing the fit threshold for both strings. The 125px English column still cannot hold “Search products” on one line.

critique.good: The wider English column keeps “Search products” on one line; identifiers and headers remain intact, and Arabic stays legible.
critique.problems: Japanese strands one character in each of the first two rows, while Chinese also strands a character in the empty-cart row and takes three lines for the email message. The extra English width produces little height benefit because Arabic still wraps in the search row.
critique.cause: The 135px English allocation takes space from Chinese and Japanese: 110px and 125px respectively fall below useful fit thresholds for those strings.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: The language columns have usable space, but nearly every key breaks across lines, often in the middle of an identifier. That makes the row labels difficult to scan.

r1C.why: Keys remain intact and Chinese has reasonable space, but the narrow Arabic column forces the error message onto three lines and splits the shipping range across lines.

ref_auto.why: Intact keys and a wider Arabic column support scanning, though the narrow Chinese column leaves a single character on a line in the cart message and spreads the error over three lines.

r3A.why: Keys remain intact, and the language columns are balanced around their content. Short messages mostly stay on one line, while longer translations wrap without excessive fragmentation.

r2B.why: Keys are intact and Chinese and Arabic have useful space, but the narrow Japanese column wraps even short messages, leaving single characters on lines and making rows taller.

r1B.why: The wider English column keeps the search phrase together, but Chinese wraps short text awkwardly and Arabic splits the shipping range across lines. Keys remain intact.

raw.unsure: D and C are close; the preference depends partly on whether the wider Arabic column in C outweighs its more fragmented Chinese text.

r1C.why: Keys remain intact, and the language columns have a useful balance. The Arabic shipping range wraps awkwardly, and several translations need multiple lines.

ref_equal.why: The narrow key column breaks every identifier, often in the middle of words, making rows harder to find and compare despite the generous language columns.

r1B.why: Keys stay intact and English has room, but the narrow Chinese column creates short fragments, while the Arabic shipping range wraps awkwardly.

ref_auto.why: Intact keys and more room for Arabic make the table readable, though the narrow Chinese column produces several short lines.

r3A.why: Keys stay intact, Chinese avoids the shortest fragments seen in C and D, and Arabic has room for the shipping range. Japanese and some English phrases still wrap.

r2B.why: Keys and Chinese read well, but the narrow Japanese column breaks even short phrases across lines, leaving isolated characters and disrupting row rhythm.

raw.unsure: A and E are close; the relative value of extra Japanese versus Arabic width depends on which translations readers compare most often.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
